items.object: The performance-to-efficiency trade-off in post-Transformer sequence models
items.answer: This is like one of the fundamental concepts of all of these alternate sequence models or post-Transformer models. items.question: How do you think about the trade-off involved in using structured matrices in neural networks?
items.object: Structured matrices as efficient representations for neural networks
items.answer: So I spent many years basically first working in a purely theoretical context on a concept called structured matrices. The idea is basically all matrices are everywhere in machine learning, and these kind of use up the bulk of the parameters and computation in neural networks. Structured matrices are basically any type of matrix that can be represented in fewer parameters. And so there's many, many different types of these, from things such as sparsity to low rank to many, many more types. And one example that I and my labmate and close collaborator Tri Dao have worked on are things called Butterfly matrices, which later led to what's called Monarch matrices. These are all just different representations of matrices that can be represented in fewer parameters. They're less expressive and more structured, which means they could have better bias or fit for certain types of problems, and overall they can be made a lot more efficient. So I spent quite a while working on this, developing different classes of structured matrices and developing algorithms for them, such as matrix multiplication that can be done faster than the bound for unstructured dense matrices. This was pretty detached from applications, but later on I spent a while trying to apply them in neural networks. The obvious way is just that everywhere you see giant matrix multiplications in your networks, you can instead replace them with structured matrices that can work with much more efficiently.

items.question: How do you approach the problem of giving sequence models very long context?
items.object: Long-context sequence modeling with recurrent models
items.answer: So actually the very first time I started working on sequence models, that was the main motivation, and I kind of liked this approach of using recurrent models from the very beginning. Of course, I was aware of what was happening in Transformers space, but there was something that was nice about the recurrent approach that I always liked. So I always spent a lot of time and effort trying to understand that more deeply and making it work. The very first question I was trying to address was actually in the context of RL, and it was about long-term credit assignment. The realization there was just that if you can fit your RL trajectory in the context of the sequence model, that's kind of enough, and then you just need to figure out how to make your model able to actually learn the dynamics across that extended length. Before Transformers, people were really working on this a lot in RNN land, and then Transformers came along and they have particularly good ways of doing this, but kind of at the expense of efficiency. A lot of my work has been trying to still target some of these interesting conceptual questions, like are there these new capabilities that we can get while also preserving efficiency and trying to do it in the right way?

items.question: How do you assess the view that model architecture has been solved because Transformers work well across so many tasks?
items.object: The view that Transformers have solved model architecture
items.answer: I think actually before we start talking about post-Transformer architectures, one aspect that is useful to draw some nuance on is about what sort of tasks do we care about or what sort of capabilities do we care about. I say that because I think there's kind of a mindset these days that the architecture of models has kind of been solved and, like, attention is all you need. People are throwing Transformers pretty much everywhere, and for the most part it does work really well in lots of places. But actually I think that's not quite accurate, and there's more nuance there. What's happening more is that different types of models are good on different types of data, and people are finding ways to transform their data in ways that are amenable for Transformers. When people are using Transformers everywhere, that's ignoring the other processing aspects and so on of what else is happening in the data.

items.object: Attention for perceptual modalities such as audio, video, and images

items.question: Why do you see attention as better suited to tokenized data than to raw, high-resolution images, audio, or video?
items.object: Attention's suitability for raw perceptual data versus tokenized data
items.answer: It's a little tricky to describe. Perhaps one way I can try to explain it is that attention, the way we use it in machine learning, is called softmax attention, and one can view that as an approximation to hard attention. In the extreme case, you can imagine that you have a big sequence or set of things, and hard attention would be an operation where I need to pick out one of these things and use that for my next layer. Softmax attention is basically an approximation where it can theoretically attend to one thing, but also it's taking a soft average over things. Really, that's kind of the spirit of attention. When you're dealing with things like language that's very chunked into abstract concepts, sometimes you will need to pay attention to this one word in my sentence as the thing I need to pay attention to to understand whatever my task is or to pass into the next layer. But when you're dealing with a really high-resolution image, it doesn't really make sense to say that what I want is some attention mechanism that's going to pick out one pixel in this image and pay attention to that one. This is also related to compressibility. Attention is very non-compressible. What it does is it stores a cache or a map of all possible things and allows you to pick and choose any one of them out of it. Other models try to compress your data into smaller latent representations, and that's really what you need when you're dealing with super high-dimensional raw data, like a super high-resolution image. That high-resolution image is extremely compressible; that's why we have such good compression algorithms that have been handcrafted in the past. You can view other types of models as also doing some form of compression and extracting features out of them, which attention is really not doing because attention is about storing the raw data and leaving it as a database or a retrieval thing that you can pick and choose things out of or attend to. The way that many end-to-end pipelines are set up is that there's some different model that works on the raw data. It could be handcrafted, or it could be other types of neural networks, such as convolutions, which are still very good for working with high-resolution data such as raw audio waveforms or high-resolution images or videos. Some flavors of state space models are also very good for that sort of data. Then the way the end-to-end pipelines work is that you often first have a different model, such as a convolutional model, learn some sort of compressed representation of the high-resolution data, and then kind of tokenize it or discretize it in some way. People talk about patching the data and stuff like that. That's all done by some form of convolution or some other type of model. Only when you've tokenized things in a sense is attention really good for working on tokens.

items.question: How do you think about choosing the level of data representation at which attention and Transformers work best?

If you can get your data processed into a state where you're working over these units of tokens, where each token really has an intrinsic meaning, maybe they can be composed, and if you've gotten your data into the form where that is the actual unit you want to reason over, then that's where attention shines. items.question: Why do you think the choice of tokenizer matters so much for Transformer language models?
items.object: Tokenization and character-level modeling in Transformers
items.answer: For language modeling in the past, people would care about all these different regimes or settings: word-level language modeling or character-level language modeling. These would be treated as different regimes. Nowadays we kind of throw away that distinction, and the token is part of the model, just another hyperparameter almost. You don't really classify things in different settings, like, “Oh, I care about character-level modeling or word-level modeling.” People used to care about that, and that does have different behaviors. For example, it's been observed that the tokenizer matters a lot for modern language models. I think maybe that's related to the idea that certain types of models such as Transformers really work best when your data has been processed into the cleanest possible level of representation, or intermediate language, in terms of which tokens are the most meaningful. If you had to constrain yourself to work purely on character level, then they start working worse. One intuition there is that it's the wrong unit of representation, the wrong type of tokenization. You would never really imagine yourself as a human reading a block of text and paying hard attention to one individual character in a word. Sometimes you do—spaces are important characters—but for the most part we don't think like that. We've already chunked things into different, higher-level representations that we then reason over. Similarly, having that correct representation is extremely important for Transformers, and that's one of the things that alternate models are better at and one of the things that they try to address.

items.question: How do you understand the tradeoff that attention creates in autoregressive Transformer language models?
items.object: Attention in autoregressive Transformer language models
items.answer: I think it's useful to think about what is the role of attention and what is the issue with it. The idea is that attention is this operation where you look at your sequence of data, like your sentence or your corpus or document, and for every single word or token in your sequence, it's going to look at that and compare it to every single other token in the sequence, do some pattern matching or something, and use that to figure out what it should attend to elsewhere and use that to transform your representation for the next layer. This is a very flexible, powerful mechanism, which is why it works so well and has been the thing that everyone uses. There's not really any other model—even all these alternate models don't really capture that idea of storing every single other word or token that you've seen and using it as a database so that you can inform your next thing. Let's focus on the setting of autoregressive language modeling, which is how GPT works and perhaps the most important setting right now. The idea is that in autoregressive modeling, you're trying to use your model to predict the next word step by step. The way I like to abstract things now is that any autoregressive model has a state, which is its representation of all the previous context it's seen. As you're trying to predict or generate the next word, you have some state that's representing everything that you've generated or seen so far. What the Transformer does is it stores every single thing. Its state is basically a cache, what's called the KV cache, which is basically a cache of everything it's seen before in the sequence. Then the Transformer can use it; it can attend to or pick and choose which previous words it has seen that it wants to use to process or predict the next word. For some types of applications, you really just can't get away with anything other than this mechanism. For example, if you wanted to just copy a large block of text, you can't do anything other than storing that entire block of text. That's why attention is indispensable even now and why it's necessary. The issue is basically that for the majority of cases it is extremely wasteful, because you're storing every single thing you've seen, and it's just not a good use of your representation power.

items.question: How do you assess convolutional language models as an approach to the efficiency problem that post-Transformer architectures are trying to solve?
items.object: Post-Transformer architectures and the limitations of convolutions for language modeling
items.answer: All of these so-called post-Transformer architectures are aiming to preserve the best parts of the Transformer while addressing this limitation of efficiency, and in particular trying to see in what cases you cannot literally cache everything you've seen. That's a useful way to think about what all of the alternatives do. Most of them have moved toward this stateful or recurrent model that has a state, which is a compressed representation of everything the model has seen, and then finding ways to define the state update mechanism that can compress the state and leverage it in the future. Even before Transformers, people were using recurrent models like RNNs. In the middle, people started using models like convolutions. There were two works that kind of simultaneously started trying to use convolutions for language modeling: one was the CK convolution, or continuous kernel convolution, by David Romero, and the other one was the line of work that I worked on. Normal convolutions don't really work well for language because they have local context. What we were trying to do was use global convolutions that have an infinitely long sliding window that can work over the entire sequence's past. This did improve over some earlier attempts, but I think I quickly realized that these models suffered from the issue that they were not flexible enough. Attention stores a cache of every word you've seen in the past and can pick and choose which one of these words to attend over at every single time step. It's very flexible in terms of which words it's attending over. The issue with convolutions is that they're doing this clumsy thing where a convolution basically says, “I'm always going to take the combination of my last, say, K words with the same linear weights.” You're taking a linear sum of your last words; those weights don't change. This is very different from the way attention can flexibly choose any one of them and have the selectivity that an attention model would have.

items.question: How do you understand the mathematical connection between gating in recurrent neural networks and discretization in state space models?
items.object: Gating mechanisms and discretization in state space models
items.answer: The idea of recurrent models, even older things like LSTMs, is how can you take your context and compress it into a state, perhaps selectively, where you can pick and choose the right information you want into your state, and then how can you use your state to selectively produce the next output or use it for whatever task you care about? This was something I had been working on from the very first time I started sequence modeling. Back when I started working on it in 2019, I was working on something called gating mechanisms, which is something people were using in RNNs from a long time ago, like from the LSTM in the early '90s. The idea is that you have a recurrent state that's evolving through time, and you want to gate something that controls the flow of information into your state. You have a recurrent state and then a new input, and you ask yourself: how do I combine my input with my state to produce my next state for a future time step? The gate is something that controls how much of the input do I let into this state? I was working on this quite early on, and my work on state space models can be seen as an evolution of those ideas that slowly refined them into this purer concept of the SSM. Ever since the beginning, I had wanted to try to figure out the cleanest mathematical way of defining gates. This is what led to this concept of discretization in state space models, which is a little bit in the weeds, but it turns out that there's very nice mathematical foundations for where gates and RNNs come about. It basically turns out to be exactly equivalent to this concept of a discretization, which is kind of saying how long do I wait in between, how much time has elapsed in between inputs. You can imagine if too much time has elapsed, then you've kind of forgotten your old state and you're kind of resetting your state and focusing on a new input. If not enough time has elapsed, then that means that each input you're looking at is individually not that important, so you don't pay attention to it as much.

items.question: What do you see as the central breakthrough behind Mamba?
items.object: Selectivity as Mamba's central breakthrough
items.answer: Long story short, there are a lot of principles I was thinking of for how to incorporate selectivity. At the same time that the SSM line of work was developing, another group was working on a model called RWKV, another recurrent model that was also trying to incorporate some early ideas of selection. It turns out they were also more or less using convolutional models, though, so they kind of suffered from the same fundamental issues but had some architectural changes that made it better in some settings. Selectivity was one of the big breakthroughs, which was exactly what Mamba was about. items.question: How did you approach restoring selectivity to state space models while keeping them efficient on GPUs?
items.object: Selectivity and GPU efficiency in state space models
items.answer: Originally I didn't want to use parameters that were static along the sequence, but I introduced this for the first state space model S4 because it was the only way to make it efficient enough. These are learnable parameters, but no matter what data you see, they're always going to be constant. After realizing that we were never going to be able to address language modeling properly, I tried to go back and see how can we reintroduce this concept but make it faster. After the first SSM paper there were a bunch of other simplifications that people did, including Anil Gupta, and I found a way to make diagonal SSMs work and basically simplify the structure of the model in a bunch of ways while still retaining its performance. Finally, with all these simplifications, I was able to reintroduce this concept of gates or selectivity in a way that was still efficient enough. I collaborated with my friend Tri, who is famously the creator of FlashAttention, and with his expertise on how to make things really efficient on hardware we were able to create a recurrent model that still had selectivity and all the other advantages of state space models, in terms of the flexibility of their state having a large expressive state that could try to compress the context by incorporating what goes into your state in a better, more data-dependent way, and doing that in a way that could still be run efficiently on a GPU. That was a bunch of things tied together, including how do you define your model in the right way that is as simple as possible while still having all of the capabilities that we were targeting? The main change was making the transition parameters data-dependent instead of constant. When doing this you lose the convolutional equivalence, and you lose the efficiency. We found an alternate way to do it by developing custom kernels targeted for GPU and materializing these states in the right part of the GPU to make it efficient enough. A lot of this was Tri's work on the efficiency and hardware algorithms to make this implementable.

items.question: How do you think about choosing the right state size for a state space model?
items.object: State size in state space models
items.answer: The idea behind a state space model is finding a state that's the exact right size that can remember all the information you care about, or is large enough to store a compression of your history. A minimum compression is kind of what we're after. We want a state that's large enough that for our task we can compress all the data exactly into the right size, but you can't have it too small, because it's going to be too lossy. If it's too big, then you're less efficient. The state is exactly this, whereas with attention you are remembering things that you saw as opposed to a compression of it. You don't really have control over what you're storing in your attention, and so that's one of the big differences with these state space models and other recurrent models in general: you have this controllable knob that controls the trade-off between efficiency versus how much can you remember. That's one of the main things I think state space models introduced over other types of recurrent models. Especially compared to older RNNs pre-Transformer, people didn't really think about this concept of how large the state was. Even a lot of the alternate models around this time weren't really paying attention to how large the state was. This idea that the state is a very important part of the model in terms of what it's remembering is interesting.

items.question: How do you distinguish the way state space models compress history from the way efficient attention mechanisms do it?
items.object: History compression in state space models versus efficient attention
items.answer: There are ways to compress the Transformer's state a lot as well, and they work differently. The way that SSMs compress state is that they don't really remember a notion of keeping track of which time step or which token it has seen in the past. It kind of squishes them all together into some abstract state that hopefully the model has learned to encode in the way that's as good for the model as possible. It's a bit of a black box. We try to give the model a flexible mechanism and guide the model toward learning what we want it to learn, but at the end of the day, we have no idea whether it is disentangled, actually remembering that this thing is this word in the past, and so on. Attention does that by design, and there are many efficient attention variants that in some ways are still the core idea of attention: it is doing some cache of the history. A lot of the efficient variants will just find, for example, the controllable knob: if I want to make it more efficient, which tokens in the past am I storing? Sliding-window attention is a variant that's pretty popular right now, saying I'm just going to remember my last, say, 1,000 tokens. Then you can get into other types of attention structures that remember some sort of strided version of this, where you remember things farther back in the past but forget at a coarse-grained resolution, or you can have other sorts of adaptive attention mechanisms that try to be more clever in picking and choosing which things they're remembering in the past. items.question: How do you think about optimal compression as a guiding principle for state space models?
items.object: Optimal compression and the limitations of state space models
items.answer: People have also realized that there is a fundamental limitation to any of these models, in that the paradigm here is basically: how do you do a form of optimal compression? That's the idea I just mentioned: how do you remember exactly what you need to remember? I think that's a core question needed to really optimize your efficiency-to-performance trade-off. That's the most salient question to me. There are definitely some types of capabilities or applications where the optimal part of that trade-off is that you just have to remember everything. There are some niche applications or capabilities, such as if you just need to literally memorize your whole document so that you can regurgitate it in the future, and then you have no choice but to memorize that entire document. Another issue people bring up is an issue with stateful models: once you've decided what's in your state, going forward you can't go back and retrieve the thing that needs to be in your state again. As a human, I can think of my brain as a sort of stateful model, and once I've forgotten something there's no way to recover that memory. That's by definition the way a state works. This is one limitation of state space models as well. The hope is that when it's trained on enough data and the right data, it will know what is important to encode or not, the same way humans can't remember everything but have learned to encode what's important and filter out or forget irrelevant things. That is probably important to intelligence. The fundamental question in terms of the efficiency-to-performance trade-off is that compression is fundamental to that. That's why lots of people have started moving toward these hybrid models where the bulk of the work is done by a stateful model and at the same time incorporating a small amount of vanilla attention, which you can think of as a perfect memorization of the model's context.

items.question: How do you think about the importance of the particular selectivity mechanism used in Mamba-style recurrent stateful models?
items.object: Selectivity mechanisms in Mamba-style recurrent stateful models
items.answer: I think that kind of just relates to the general question: what is the best state update mechanism? How do you design a mechanism for how your state evolves over time, and how is it incorporating new information? All of that is a form of selectivity, and the question is what is the best one that has the best ability to process data while also being efficiently implementable? My current feeling is that once people started incorporating the selectivity and the state expansion that Mamba started doing, most of them seem quite similar in performance. I don't know that there's qualitatively different performance. For example, in the gap between older RNNs like LSTMs versus Transformers, there was a qualitative shift in the ability of these models. Now with some of the more recent recurrent stateful models, there was also a qualitatively different or new type of mechanism that has been explored. Within that space, the work so far seems pretty similar; most of them seem pretty similar. It almost seems like any form of selectivity will be pretty reasonably similar in performance. It remains to be seen whether there's a completely different type that will have different scaling laws or whatever.

items.question: Why do you see less-processed data as a particularly promising setting for Mamba and other alternatives to Transformers?
items.object: Mamba and other alternative architectures for less-processed data
items.answer: I think one of the areas where these models are most interesting is in new modalities and things that have co-evolved less with Transformers. One simple example, even in the context of language, is I alluded to this earlier about how when we disentangle the tokenizer from the main model or force ourselves to use less optimized tokenizers, the alternative models seem to start doing way better than Transformers, especially if you're trying to match on a compute-controlled basis. The main issue with Transformers is efficiency because they're doing this wasteful storage of everything they've seen. When your data hasn't been tokenized into a nice representation, the whole point is that it only works if your data has already been compressed into a way where each unit you're storing is meaningful. That's this fuzzy notion of semantics or meaningfulness I've been talking about, because if you're not storing one meaningful unit of information, then you're just wasting space. Sasha Rush and one of his students, Junyang at Cornell, had this paper called MambaByte, which investigated what happens if you're modeling raw bytes. They basically found fairly large gaps in performance where alternate models like Mamba were significantly better than Transformers, especially when compute-matched. Hopefully this makes more intuitive sense because this data is uncompressed and the Transformer is just extremely wasteful. It seems the less processed the data is, the better some of these alternate models are at dealing with it in an elegant way and compressing it the way it needs to be done. I actually don't know if I'm aware of other groups that have reproduced that particular phenomenon. I would love to see it reproduced; it was an academic thing, and seeing it independently verified, especially at larger scale, would be very enlightening. But I've observed similar things in other modalities. In the original Mamba paper we worked on DNA, which is a language-like thing that has a small vocabulary, but it's been tokenized in a way where one token is just one DNA base pair, and there hasn't been any co-evolution of tokenizers with the architecture. Here, as a drop-in model, what we found was that Mamba was way better than Transformers there as well.

items.question: How do you think attention and Mamba-type architectures should fit into a model when a modality already has a well-tuned end-to-end pipeline?
items.object: The role of attention and Mamba-type architectures in a tuned end-to-end pipeline
items.answer: From one perspective, if you already have something that's a really nice, tuned end-to-end pipeline, maybe you should just go with it. Especially, as you were saying, the less processed the data is, the more important it is to use other types of models.

items.question: How do you view handcrafted data-processing pipelines as a long-term approach to deep learning?
items.object: Handcrafted data processing versus learning end-to-end compression and tokenization
items.answer: The question is: is that better or is it good enough? When we have really strong priors on how to process our data, should we just use that? I think it's a bit of a stopgap, because ultimately the way things should be done is everything should be as elegant and end-to-end as possible. That's kind of the whole premise and promise of deep learning. The field has evolved to slowly strip away all of these hard-coded, handcrafted definitions and processing, and it will always evolve in that direction. Hopefully one day we'll be at the point where there's something as generic and flexible as possible. From a philosophical standpoint, I think it's important to continue developing things that are more flexible and end-to-end and particularly can do this form of—hopefully we can learn the right compression, or even for a tokenizer, hopefully we can learn the right tokenizer instead of having predefined tokenization schemes, using an end-to-end model. That's kind of a philosophical answer, but even without that I think the reason why this is important is because when you have the handcrafted pipelines you'll inevitably run into issues. Maybe your handcrafted pipeline is going to address most of the issues, but then you run into other things. That's why learning everything from data is the most important, to capture the way interactions really should be.

items.question: Why do you think the problems tokenizers cause in language models support learning from raw data end-to-end?
items.object: Tokenization in language models and learning from raw data end-to-end
items.answer: I think even in language, which has been our predominant example of a data modality and its processing schemes, these are still pretty ingrained, but the community is definitely observing issues that tokenizers cause. Andrej Karpathy has a pretty viral tweet about all the issues that tokenizers cause. For example, I think it's been speculated that one of the reasons modern LLMs have a lot of trouble doing arithmetic or paying attention to basic things, like if you ask it to generate words starting with a certain letter, I think it has trouble with anything related to spelling. That seems like a big struggle for these models, and it's probably been hypothesized to be related to the tokenizer because spelling is at the level of characters, right? Tokenizers operate at a higher level than that, and so the model loses the ability to reason over characters. That's just one example of why doing things from raw data end-to-end as much as possible is, I believe, the right approach in general for machine learning.

items.question: How do you think about moving beyond tokenization toward models that learn directly from unstructured data?
items.object: Reducing tokenization and other imposed structure in machine learning
items.answer: I think there's still a little bit of work to be done to figure out how to do that, because the tokenization is there for a reason. It drastically improves efficiency and whatnot, so it's there for a reason. But the way the whole field has always evolved is that structure is there for a reason, maybe because of compute constraints, for example, or because we don't have the models for it yet. As we get more tools for it, we always want to reduce structure, use better models suited for more general, unstructured data, put in more compute, and have things learned end-to-end and as automatically as possible. It's always the way things should be done to really learn.

items.question: Where do you see the theoretical understanding of Mamba-style sequence models leading next?
items.object: Theoretical frameworks and extensions for Mamba-style sequence models
items.answer: There's a lot of ongoing things. One thing I mentioned is continuing to improve the core mechanisms. Then there's a lot of work to be done in understanding them still. For example, Mamba-2 was an improvement to Mamba for efficiency, but actually a lot of it was developing new theoretical frameworks for understanding sequence models. As I mentioned, for example, relating them to structured matrices and structured matrix transformations on sequences. I think it's just getting started in terms of the developments that occur downstream of that. Even my students at Carnegie Mellon have been working on lots of different extensions and applications of these things. For example, from sequences, which can be viewed as one example of a simple graph structure—when your data is structured in a sequential order—how can you generalize this to other forms of graphical structures with different types of dependencies? One of the things we've worked on is extending it to other types of graphical structures. Another related thing is how do you extend these to bidirectional sequence modeling in the most natural way? That's something one of my students is going to release very soon, hopefully this week.

items.question: How do you think existing Transformer work should inform the development of post-Transformer models?
items.object: Using existing Transformer work to develop post-Transformer models
items.answer: There's a whole class of problems about how can we leverage the existing work done for Transformers to improve all of these other models. This includes model design, of course, which is one thing we want to try to do, but also how do you actually use the pretrained models, which have been scaled to very large, powerful models? How can we use them to bootstrap the space of post-Transformer models in a way that we don't have to reinvent the wheel entirely? I think this is a very important and interesting direction as well. For example, my group has also started working on distillation techniques for how can you take a pretrained Transformer model and convert it into a state model with a much smaller amount of training. These are examples of big general problems.
